extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, students of PR, organizational leaders seeking guidance on shaping public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for counsel on public relations: how to analyze publics, choose media and tactics, craft messages, stage events, and mobilize opinion to shape or crystallize public opinion. Illustrated by concrete historical examples and techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the public relations counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel directs and supervises the activities of his clients wherever they impinge upon the daily life of the public. He interprets the client to the public, and he interprets the public to the client. His advice is given on all occasions on which his client appears before the public, whether it be in concrete form or as an idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: advising hotels, magazines, corporations, governments; acting on advertising, lectures, the stage, the pulpit, the newspaper, the photograph, the wireless, the mail or any other form of thought communication. Emphasizes that counsel’s work touches intimate aspects of daily life and may be varied and non-formulaic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reach the public only through established mediums of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The public can be reached only through established mediums of communication' (advertising, lectures, the stage, the pulpit, the newspaper, the photograph, the wireless, the mail or any other form of thought communication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the appropriate medium(s) for the target public; examples show using newspapers, national press services, Associated Press, radio, motion pictures, and mailing distribution. Use the medium that best carries the intended implication to that particular public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide positive, concrete evidence to counter rumors or doubts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere denial will accomplish little against damaging rumors; the only way to overcome a rumor is to give the public some positive evidence of the intention or fact you wish to establish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hotel example: renew engagement of a nationally known maître d’hôtel for years and publicize it so the public believes the hotel will not close. Anti-pattern: issuing only denials without demonstrable, newsworthy actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make existing valuable content accessible to new target publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify valuable editorial/material assets and extend their appeal by repackaging and distributing to audiences who would find them interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magazine example: take an interesting article, base a nationwide inquiry on it among business/professional men, collate and distribute the abstract to newspapers and class journals; leverage endorsements and lectures to draw international attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use credible experts/authorities to validate claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage authority of experts to make a proposition articulate and believable to the public (e.g., dietetic or medical endorsements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Packing house/bacon example: have a physician undertake a survey showing hearty breakfasts are dietetically sound and publicize findings to increase general demand. Radium bank example: found an institution (First National Radium Bank) to create an impression of availability for medical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobilize opinion leaders and influential groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the opinions of recognized leaders or influential group members articulate and public; their expressed opinions will shape broader public sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hair-net example: survey club women leaders and publish their opinions to influence fashion trends; use prominent national figures (e.g., Enrico Caruso) to influence foreign audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct exhaustive study and segment audiences; tailor messages to different publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform exhaustive study of the subject and divide material into categories based on the publics to which it will appeal; prepare different presentations for ethnologists, language students, sports fans, women, senators, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lithuania campaign: tailored facts and presentations for each audience segment (ethnology, language, sports, senators, House members), plus coordinated events (mass meetings, petitions, delegations) and use of multiple media. Emphasizes audience-specific framing and content selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert factual/scholarly material into interesting news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly treatises or accurate studies should be made into interesting stories of news value to gain popular attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roumania example: transform historically correct and ethnologically accurate treatises into interesting news stories to reach the public; avoid merely publishing treatises that the public will ignore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage visible, demonstrative events and ceremonies with notable persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Create dramatized events involving prominent figures and produce motion and still pictures so the event becomes news and conveys the intended message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piave launching, inter-city radio inauguration with mayors, Metropolitan Opera performance for Belgian royalty—use prominent participants and photographs/film to spread the intended implication domestically and internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use coordinated multi-channel campaigns for broad effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ all avenues of approach—mail, lecture platform, newspaper advertising, radio, motion pictures, petitions, press associations—to capitalize public interest and bring about official recognition or action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lithuania example demonstrates synchronized use of press, radio, motion pictures, advertising, mass meetings, and petitions. Plan campaigns phase by phase to educate and mobilize target publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make claims credible by demonstrating them rather than merely proclaiming them
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of simply proclaiming desirable attributes, prove contentions by concrete action that illustrates the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real estate example: to sell coöperative apartments to a high-class clientele, make the community an active center for cultural and civic manifestations (e.g., open a post office with national figures attending) so the claim is evidenced, not just asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and publicize symbolic endorsements, citations, and visible signs of commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use certificates, citations, public displays and simultaneous announcements by respected authorities or groups to influence behavior and encourage imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reemployment campaign: prepare citations signed by Secretaries of War and Navy for display by employers who pledged to re-employ ex-service men; coordinate public display dates to maximize imitation and spur wider action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose public perception through interviews and literature review before intervening
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze causes of unfavorable public opinion by talking to representative groups and examining literature and press attacks; use this diagnosis to design remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York hospitality example: interviewed visitors and representatives of groups, reviewed literature and criticisms, discovered belief that New York was 'cold and inhospitable', then formed Welcome Stranger Committee to counteract perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt product/service offerings to meet public needs and publicize changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify unmet or latent public wants and modify offerings accordingly, then publicize such changes so the public is aware and responds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Waldorf-Astoria instituted special children's menus after discovering desire for special foods; publicized change and gained favorable comment and business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use surveys and collated responses as publicity material
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission or use surveys among target groups, collate and analyze responses, and distribute abstracts or symposia gratis to newspapers and organizations to stimulate interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magazine used a physician-led inquiry of business/professional men and distributed the findings widely; organizations reprinted the symposium and distributed it because of intrinsic interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form broad, non-partisan coalitions to portray unified support
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemble representatives from diverse political and social groups into unified committees to make disinterested and unified appeals that reflect broad support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: League of Nations example: formed a non-partisan committee of women representing many affiliations to make a united appeal; used meeting to dramatize disinterested and unified national support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use visual imagery and mass photography/press to amplify implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage photographs and press imagery of staged events to convey implications about unity, support, or prestige to a wide audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belgian royal visit: Metropolitan Opera performance photographed and printed worldwide to show national elements’ affection; images carried the intended message beyond the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan appeals that capitalize on latent or passive public sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify latent opinions and arouse or give them voice through authoritative statements or events so the sentiment becomes active and influential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hair-net example: club women’s expressed opinion awakened a latent opinion favoring long hair and thus moderated the bobbed-hair vogue. Emphasizes converting passive sentiment into articulated public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: avoid reliance on mere denial or isolated statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Denials or isolated statements, no matter how vigorous or widely disseminated, are often ineffective in changing public opinion without corroborating action or evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated across examples (hotel rumor, Roumania treatises) — prefer demonstrable actions, newsworthy events, expert validation, or broad campaigns rather than simple denials.
